title: Kerala High Court: Trademark Suits Must Go to the District Court, Whatever the Claim Is Worth
meta_description: Kerala High Court rules a trademark infringement suit cannot be tried below the District Court even if its value fits a Munsiff Court's pecuniary limit.
case_name: Cutis International Cosmetics Clinic & Ors. v. Cutis Institute of Medicine and Surgery
body: Two clinics sharing the word 'Cutis' in their names ended up fighting not over whether one had copied the other's mark, but over which court in Kerala was even allowed to hear that fight. Cutis Institute of Medicine and Surgery sued Cutis International Cosmetics Clinic and its directors for trademark infringement, and the defendants tried to have the case shunted down to a Munsiff Court before the merits were ever touched.

The reason the defendants thought they had a shot at a lower court was the size of the claim. The plaint valued the suit at Rs 5,10,000, made up of a nominal Rs 1,000 for the injunction and Rs 5,00,000 in damages, a figure that comfortably sits within what a Munsiff Court in Kerala can ordinarily try. Relying on Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 11(2) of the Kerala Civil Courts Act, the defendants filed an application arguing that a suit of this value belongs in the lowest court competent to try it, not the District Court where it had been filed.

Justice Mohammed Nias C.P. was not persuaded. The judge held that Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 carves trademark suits out of the ordinary rule entirely. That section requires a suit for infringement to be instituted in a District Court having jurisdiction, and the Court treated that requirement as fixing a floor below which no trademark suit can go, regardless of how modest the damages claimed happen to be. Pecuniary value, which normally decides where a civil suit lands in the hierarchy of courts, simply has no role to play once the cause of action is trademark infringement.

The ruling went further than just naming the right forum. The defendants had also floated a fallback position, arguing that even if the suit had to be filed in the District Court, it could still be handed down to a Munsiff Court for trial, keeping institution and adjudication separate. The Court rejected that too, holding that a suit's place of institution and its place of trial cannot be prised apart on a party's say-so. That separation can only happen through a lawful transfer ordered by the District Court itself, or because some other statute specifically allows it, and neither existed here.

Section 134, on this reading, effectively treats the District Court as the lowest court competent to try a trademark suit for the purposes of Section 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 15 ordinarily tells a plaintiff to sue in the lowest grade of court that can handle the claim, but where a special statute names a particular forum, that naming overrides the general civil procedure default. The Trade Marks Act does exactly that, and the Court declined to read Section 9 of the CPC as creating a backdoor around a jurisdictional bar Parliament had deliberately written into the special statute.

Defendants in trademark disputes sometimes keep the damages figure in a plaint deliberately low, hoping a smaller claim will land the case in a subordinate court with a different pace, different procedure, or simply a longer road for the plaintiff to travel before trial even begins. This order shuts that door in Kerala. Once a plaint pleads infringement under the Trade Marks Act, the case sits with the District Court or above no matter what number appears in the valuation column, and no procedural manoeuvre at the trial stage can move it.

For brand owners litigating in Kerala, the practical lesson is to file directly at the District Court and resist any temptation to undervalue the suit for speed or convenience, since the forum question is settled in the plaintiff's favour from the outset. For defendants weighing their options, a jurisdictional challenge built purely on the size of the claim is no longer worth the paper it is filed on, as this revision petition shows even a suit worth little more than five lakh rupees stays exactly where the Trade Marks Act puts it.
why_it_matters: Businesses sued for trademark infringement in Kerala, or anywhere the same reading of Section 134 is followed, cannot use a modest damages claim to push the case down to a Munsiff Court. Brand owners filing suit should go straight to the District Court regardless of valuation, and defendants should expect a jurisdictional objection based on claim size to fail, since Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act fixes the forum independent of what the plaint seeks in damages.
card_summary: Kerala High Court holds that a trademark infringement suit must be tried by the District Court or above, even where the damages claimed fall within a Munsiff Court's pecuniary limit.
card_tip: Do not rely on a low damages figure to argue a trademark suit belongs in a subordinate court: Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act fixes the District Court as the floor, regardless of valuation.
verification_notes: Case name, suit valuation (Rs 5,10,000), the defendants' reliance on Section 9 CPC and Section 11(2) of the Kerala Civil Courts Act, and the core holding that trademark suits cannot be tried below the District Court regardless of pecuniary value are confirmed across LiveLawBiz, Conventus Law and SupremeToday.ai. The judge's name (Mohammed Nias C.P., J.) and the rejection of the argument separating institution from trial are drawn from the same reports. Sources differ slightly on the exact decision date, with one giving 8 September 2026 and LiveLaw's own report dated 11 September 2026; this article uses the earlier date given directly as the decision date and notes the discrepancy here rather than treating it as settled.
